title:
Zhang Fei in rage whips the Investigator
He Jin plots to destroy the eunuchs
paragraphs: Now [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), styled Zhongying, was a man of Lintao in Longxi, Grand Administrator of [Hedong](loc-hedong), arrogant by nature. He had slighted [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) that day, and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), his temper up, would have cut the man down. Liu Bei and [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) held him back. "The man is the court's own officer. Who are you to kill him?" Zhang Fei said: "If I do not kill the wretch, I must stay and take his orders instead, and that I cannot stomach! Stay here if you like, brothers, but I will go elsewhere alone!" "We three swore to live and die together," said Liu Bei. "How should we part? Better we all go elsewhere." "That will ease my anger a little," said Zhang Fei.

So the three marched their men through the night and joined [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), who treated them handsomely. They put their armies together and went on against [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao). [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) was at that time with [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) against [Zhang Liang](char-zhang-liang), and they fought a great battle at Quyang. Zhang Bao had eighty or ninety thousand men camped behind a hill. Zhu Jun made [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) his vanguard and sent him against them, and Zhang Bao sent out his lieutenant Gao Sheng to offer battle. Liu Bei set [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) on him. Zhang Fei put his horse forward with his spear leveled, and they had not fought many bouts when he ran Gao Sheng through and the man fell from his horse. Liu Bei waved his men on to the charge. Then Zhang Bao, still mounted, loosed his hair, took sword in hand, and began his sorcery. Wind and thunder broke out, and a black vapor came down from the sky with what seemed an endless host riding in it. Liu Bei pulled his men back in haste, his ranks fell into confusion, and he came off the field beaten. He took counsel with Zhu Jun. "He works sorcery," said Zhu Jun. "Tomorrow we kill pigs, sheep and dogs, take their blood, and set men in hiding along the hilltop. When the rebels come on in pursuit, we pour it down from the high ground, and his spell can be broken."

On [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun)'s orders [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) sent [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) with a thousand men apiece to lie hidden on the high ridge behind the hill, with the blood of pigs, sheep and dogs and other filth made ready. Next day [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao) came out with flags shaking and drums beating to offer battle, and Liu Bei rode out to meet him. As the two sides closed, Zhang Bao worked his spell. Wind and thunder broke, sand flew and stones rolled, a black vapor filled the sky, and men and horses came pouring down out of it. Liu Bei turned his horse and fled, and Zhang Bao drove his men after him. As they came over the crest the men in hiding fired the signal shot and flung the filth down all together. Paper men and straw horses came tumbling out of the air to the ground; the wind and thunder stopped at once, and no more sand flew. Zhang Bao saw the spell broken and would have drawn off, but Guan Yu came out on the left and Zhang Fei on the right, with Liu Bei and Zhu Jun close on his heels, and the rebels were routed. Liu Bei caught sight of the banner of the [General of Earth](char-zhang-bao) and rode hard after it. Zhang Bao took to the wilds, and an arrow of Liu Bei's caught him in the left arm. He escaped with the arrow still in him, fled into Yangcheng, and shut himself up there. Zhu Jun ringed the city about and laid siege to it, and sent men for news of [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song).

The scouts came back with the whole of it. [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) had won a great victory. After [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s repeated defeats the court had put Huangfu Song in his place. By the time he came up [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) was dead and [Zhang Liang](char-zhang-liang) had the command of his people, holding out against the imperial army. Huangfu Song beat him seven times running and cut him down at Quyang. Zhang Jiao's coffin was opened, the body mutilated and the head struck off and sent to the capital, and the rest surrendered. The court had raised Huangfu Song to General of Chariots and Cavalry with the governorship of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province), and he had memorialized further that [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) had merit and no fault, so that Lu Zhi was restored to his old office. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) too was rewarded, with the chancellorship of Jinan, and was to march off that same day to take it up. On this news [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) pressed his men forward and threw everything against Yangcheng. The rebels were in desperate straits, and their own officer Yan Zheng stabbed [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao), brought in his head, and surrendered. So Zhu Jun pacified several commanderies and sent up word of the victory.

Three more of the Yellow Turban remnant were up by now — [Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong), [Han Zhong](char-han-zhong) and [Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) — who had gathered tens of thousands, burned and plundered wherever they came, and claimed to be avenging [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao). The court ordered [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) to take his victorious army against them at once. The rebels held [Wancheng](loc-wancheng), and Zhu Jun brought his men up to attack it. Zhao Hong sent Han Zhong out to fight, and Zhu Jun sent [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) with [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) against the southwest corner. Han Zhong took the whole of his best troops to the southwest to meet them, while Zhu Jun himself loosed two thousand armored horse straight at the northeast. The rebels, afraid for the city, left the southwest in haste and turned back. Liu Bei fell on their rear and broke them, and they fled into Wancheng. Zhu Jun divided his men and ringed the place on all four sides. Grain ran out within, and Han Zhong sent a man out to offer surrender, which Zhu Jun would not have. "[Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) won the realm because he knew how to take a surrender and welcome the submissive," said Liu Bei. "Why refuse Han Zhong?" "That was one age and this is another," said Zhu Jun. "In the days when Qin fell and [Xiang Yu](char-xiang-yu) rose the realm was in confusion and the people had no settled master, so surrender was invited and submission rewarded, to draw men in. Now all within the seas is one, and only the Yellow Turbans are in revolt. Allow them to surrender, and nothing will be left to encourage men to good. A brigand could plunder at will while he was winning and give himself up the moment he lost. That would feed the brigand's appetite, and it is no good policy." "You are right not to take their surrender," said Liu Bei. "But we have the city ringed on every side as tight as an iron barrel. They beg to surrender and cannot, so they will fight to the death. Ten thousand men of one mind cannot be withstood, let alone the tens of thousands in there who have given their lives up for lost. Better draw off from the east and the south and attack only the northwest. They will abandon the city and run, with no heart left for fighting, and may be taken as they go."

[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) thought well of it, drew his men off the eastern and southern faces, and threw them all at the northwest. Sure enough, [Han Zhong](char-han-zhong) led out his men, abandoned the city and ran for it. Zhu Jun, with [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), brought the whole army down on them. Han Zhong was shot dead, and the rest scattered in every direction.

They were still in pursuit when [Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong) and [Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) came up with the rest of the rebels and gave battle. [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) saw how strong Zhao Hong was and drew off for the time, and Zhao Hong took the chance to retake [Wancheng](loc-wancheng). Zhu Jun camped ten li away and was making ready to attack when a body of horse appeared out of the east. At its head rode a man with a broad brow and a wide face, a tiger's body and a bear's loins, a man of Fuchun in [Wu Commandery](loc-wu-commandery): [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) by name, Wentai by style, and descended from Sun Wu. At seventeen he had gone with his father to Qiantang and seen a dozen pirates on the bank, sharing out a merchant's goods. "These robbers can be taken," he said to his father, and went up the bank blade in hand, shouting and signaling to right and left as though calling men on. The pirates thought the government troops were upon them, dropped the whole of the plunder and ran. Sun Jian went after them and killed one. His name was known through commandery and county from that day, and he was put forward for a colonelcy. Afterwards, when the sorcerer Xu Chang of [Kuaiji](loc-kuaiji) rebelled and styled himself the Yangming Emperor with tens of thousands at his back, Sun Jian and the commandery Major raised a thousand brave men and more, joined the provincial forces, and broke him, cutting down Xu Chang and his son Xu Shao. The Inspector Zang Min memorialized his service, and he was made Assistant Magistrate of Yandu, and after that of [Xuyi](loc-xuyi) and of [Xiapi](loc-xiapi). Now, with the Yellow Turbans up, he had gathered the young men of his district, some merchants and travelers, and fifteen hundred picked men from the Huai and the Si, and had come to join the fighting.

[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) was delighted. He set [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) on the south gate and [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) on the north, took the west himself, and left the east open for the rebels to flee by. Sun Jian was first up the wall and cut down a score of the rebels, and the rest broke. [Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong) spurred at him with his lance leveled. Sun Jian sprang down from the wall, tore the lance from his hands and thrust him from the saddle with it, then mounted Zhao Hong's horse and rode back and forth killing rebels. [Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) brought his men out by the north gate straight into Liu Bei, with no heart for fighting and nothing in mind but flight. Liu Bei drew and loosed, and the arrow took Sun Zhong and tumbled him from his horse. Zhu Jun's main body came up behind and fell on them, taking tens of thousands of heads, and those who surrendered were past counting. Throughout the [Nanyang](loc-nanyang) region more than ten commanderies were pacified. Zhu Jun marched back to the capital, and by edict was made General of Chariots and Cavalry and Prefect of Henan. He memorialized the services of Sun Jian, Liu Bei and the others. Sun Jian had friends at court, was given a Major's post in another commandery, and went off to take it up. But Liu Bei waited day after day and got nothing.

The three went about low in spirits, and were walking the street one day when the carriage of a court officer named Zhang Jun came by. [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) stopped him and told him what he had done in the field. Zhang Jun was aghast, and went into court to see the [Emperor](char-emperor-ling). "The Yellow Turbans rose, and the root of it was the Ten Attendants selling offices and titles, employing none but their own and punishing none but their enemies, till the realm fell into confusion. Cut down the Ten Attendants now, hang their heads in the southern suburb, send envoys to proclaim it through the realm and reward those who have served, and all within the four seas will be quiet of itself." The Ten Attendants told the Emperor that Zhang Jun was deceiving his sovereign, and the Emperor had his guards put the man out. Then they talked it over among themselves. "This comes of the men who did good service against the Yellow Turbans and got no posts for it, and now the grudge is out. Let the ministry give them some small posts for now; there will be time enough to deal with them later." So Liu Bei was made Defender of Anxi County in Zhongshan, Dingzhou, and was to take up the post by a set day. He sent his soldiers home to their villages, kept only a score of his own people about him, and came with [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) to Anxi. In a month of governing the county he had not touched so much as a hair of the people's, and they were all won over to him. From the day he took office he ate at one table with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei and slept in one bed with them. When he sat in company, the two of them stood in attendance beside him all day long and never wearied of it.

He had not been four months in the county when an edict came down that all who held office by military merit were to be weeded out, and [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) feared he was among them. The Investigator came on his round to the county just then. Liu Bei went out beyond the wall to meet him and bowed. The Investigator kept his seat on his horse and answered with a slight motion of his whip, at which [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) both took fire. At the posting house the Investigator took the high seat facing south, and Liu Bei stood below the steps. After a long while the Investigator asked him what his origin was. "I am descended from Prince Jing of Zhongshan," said Liu Bei. "From [Zhuo Commandery](loc-zhuo) onward I have cut down Yellow Turbans in thirty engagements and more, great and small, and for that small service I was given this post." The Investigator shouted at him: "You lie about your imperial kindred and invent your services! The court's edict has just come down to weed out corrupt and worthless officers like you!" Liu Bei murmured assent and withdrew. Back in the county he took counsel with his clerks. "The Investigator throws his weight about for nothing but a bribe," said a clerk. "I have not touched a hair of the people's," said Liu Bei. "Where am I to find money for him?" Next day the Investigator began by seizing the county clerks, and tried to force them to swear that the Defender had oppressed the people. Liu Bei went several times himself to plead for their release, but the gatemen turned him back every time.

Now [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) had drunk a few cups to drown his gloom, and was riding past the posting house when he saw fifty or sixty old men at the gate weeping. He asked what was the matter, and they answered: "The Investigator is forcing the clerks to ruin [Lord Liu](char-liu-bei). We came to plead for him, but they would not let us in, and the gatemen beat us and drove us off!" A great rage took Zhang Fei. His round eyes stared, he ground his teeth, and he was out of the saddle and into the posting house before the gatemen could stop him. He went straight through to the back, where the Investigator sat in the hall with the county clerks bound on the floor. "Robber of the people!" Zhang Fei roared at him. "Do you know who I am?" Before the Investigator could get a word out Zhang Fei had him by the hair, hauled him out of the posting house and up to the hitching post before the county office, tied him fast to it, broke off a willow switch, and laid it on across both his legs with a will, breaking a dozen switches one after another.

[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) was still brooding when he heard the uproar in front of the office and asked what it was. "[General Zhang](char-zhang-fei) has a man tied up before the office and is beating him." He hurried out to look, and the man tied there was the Investigator. He asked in alarm what had happened. "A robber of the people like this deserves to be beaten to death!" said [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei). "[Lord Xuande](char-liu-bei), save my life!" cried the Investigator. Liu Bei was a merciful man after all, and called sharply to Zhang Fei to stop. [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) came round from the side. "Brother, you have won great merit again and again and have only a county Defender's post for it, and now an Investigator insults you. A thicket of thorns is no place for a phoenix to roost. Kill the man, I say, give up the office and go home, and look to something larger." So Liu Bei took the seal and ribbon, hung them about the Investigator's neck, and rebuked him: "For the harm you have done the people you have earned death, but for this once I spare you. Here are the seal and ribbon. From this hour I am gone!" The Investigator reported to the Grand Administrator of Dingzhou, who sent a statement up to the provincial office, and officers went out to arrest them. The three went to Daizhou and took refuge with Liu Hui, who, seeing that Liu Bei was of the imperial house, kept them hidden in his own home.

The Ten Attendants, with the power now in their hands, agreed among themselves that any man who would not go with them should be destroyed. [Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong) and [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) sent to the officers who had broken the Yellow Turbans to demand gold and silk, and memorialized the dismissal of all who refused. [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) would give nothing, and were stripped of office for it. The [Emperor](char-emperor-ling) also made Zhao Zhong General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Zhang Rang and twelve more were made full marquises. Government rotted further and the people murmured. Then the rebel Ou Xing rose in Changsha, and Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun rebelled in Yuyang, the one calling himself Son of Heaven and the other Grand General. Urgent memorials came thick as snow, and the Ten Attendants hid every one of them and reported nothing.

One day the [Emperor](char-emperor-ling) was drinking with the Ten Attendants in the back garden when Liu Tao, Counselor Remonstrant, came straight up before him and broke into weeping. The Emperor asked the cause. "The realm may be lost within a day, and Your Majesty sits drinking with eunuchs!" said Liu Tao. "The country is at peace. Where is the danger?" "Brigands are up on every side and overrunning the provinces, and the whole of it comes of the Ten Attendants selling office, preying on the people and deceiving their sovereign. Every honest man has left the court. The ruin is before your eyes!" The Ten Attendants took off their caps and threw themselves down before the Emperor. "If the great ministers will not have us, we cannot live. We beg leave to go home to our fields with our lives, and we will give up our whole estates to help pay for the army." And they wept bitterly. The Emperor turned on Liu Tao in anger. "You have your own attendants about you. Why will you not let me have mine?" And he called the guards to take the man out and behead him. Liu Tao cried aloud as they took him: "I do not grudge my death! I grieve for the house of Han — four hundred years and more, and all of it ended in a morning!"

The guards hustled Liu Tao out and were about to strike when one of the great ministers called to them to stop. "Hold your hands until I have pleaded with His Majesty." It was Chen Dan, Minister of the Masses, and he went straight in to the [Emperor](char-emperor-ling). "What is Counselor Liu's crime, that he is to be put to death?" "He slandered my attendants and affronted my person." Chen Dan said: "The people of the realm would eat the flesh of the Ten Attendants, and Your Majesty honors them as father and mother. They have not an inch of merit among them, and every one of them is made a full marquis. [Feng Xu](char-feng-xu) besides was in league with the Yellow Turbans and would have risen inside the palace. If Your Majesty does not reflect now, the altars of the land will come down before your eyes!" "Feng Xu's treason was never proved," said the Emperor. "Are there not one or two loyal men among the Ten Attendants?" Chen Dan beat his head against the steps as he pleaded. The Emperor in anger had him dragged away, and he and Liu Tao were both put in prison, where the Ten Attendants murdered them that same night. Then they forged an edict making [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) Grand Administrator of Changsha, to put down Ou Xing.

In under fifty days word came that the victory was won and [Jiangxia](loc-jiangxia) pacified. [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) was made Marquis of Wucheng by edict, and [Liu Yu](char-liu-yu) was made Governor of [You Province](loc-you-province) and sent with troops to Yuyang against Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun. Liu Hui of Daizhou recommended [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) to Liu Yu by letter. Liu Yu was greatly pleased and made him a Commandant, and Liu Bei led his men straight to the rebels' nest, fought them for several days on end, and broke their spirit. Zhang Chun was cruel and violent through and through, and his soldiers turned against him. One of his own officers stabbed him, brought in the head, and came over with the men under him. Zhang Ju, seeing all was lost, hanged himself, and the whole of Yuyang was subdued. Liu Yu memorialized Liu Bei's great service, and the court pardoned him the whipping of the Investigator, made him Assistant Magistrate of Xiami, and then promoted him Defender of Gaotang. [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) also sent up a memorial setting out Liu Bei's earlier services, and recommended him as Major of a Detached Division and acting Magistrate of Pingyuan County. At Pingyuan Liu Bei had money, grain and troops enough, and built up his old standing again. Liu Yu, for his part in putting down the rebels, was made Grand Commandant.

In the sixth year of [Zhongping](misc-zhongping), the fourth month of summer, the [Emperor](char-emperor-ling) lay gravely ill, and called the Grand General [He Jin](char-he-jin) into the palace to settle what should come after. He Jin had risen out of a butcher's household. His sister had gone into the palace as a Noble Lady, borne a son, [Bian](char-prince-bian), and been made [Empress](char-empress-he), and from this came his own power and high office. The Emperor had also favored Lady Wang, who bore him a son, [Xie](char-prince-xie). Empress He poisoned her out of jealousy, and the boy was brought up in the palace of [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong). The Empress Dowager was the Emperor's own mother, wife of Liu Chang, Marquis of Jiedu. Emperor Huan had died without a son, and Liu Chang's son was brought in and set on the throne as Emperor Ling. On coming to the throne he brought his mother to live in the palace and honored her as Empress Dowager.

[Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) had once urged the [Emperor](char-emperor-ling) to make [Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) heir apparent, and he too doted on the boy and meant to name him. Now, as he lay gravely ill, the Attendant [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) urged him: "If Xie is to be set up, [He Jin](char-he-jin) must be killed first, to cut off future trouble." The Emperor thought well of it, and summoned He Jin to the palace. He Jin came as far as the palace gate, where Major Pan Yin said to him: "You must not go in. Jian Shuo means to murder you." He Jin took fright, hurried back to his own house, and called the great ministers together, meaning to destroy the eunuchs root and branch. One of those sitting there rose. "The power of the eunuchs goes back to the reigns of Emperors Chong and Zhi, and it has spread so wide through the court that it cannot all be cut away. If the secret leaks, your whole clan will be destroyed. I beg you to consider it closely." He Jin looked, and it was [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), a Colonel. "What does a stripling like you know of the great affairs of state?" he said sharply.

[He Jin](char-he-jin) was still hesitating when Pan Yin came in. "The Emperor is dead. [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) and the Ten Attendants have agreed to keep the death secret and send out a forged summons calling [Imperial In-law He](char-he-jin) into the palace, to cut off future trouble, and then set the prince [Xie](char-prince-xie) on the throne."

He had not finished when the summons came, calling [He Jin](char-he-jin) in at once to settle the succession. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) said: "Today we must first set the succession right, and deal with the traitors after." "Who will stand with me to set up the rightful lord and put down the traitors?" said He Jin. A man stepped out. "Give me five thousand picked men. I will cut my way in through the gates, set up the new sovereign, destroy the eunuchs to the last of them, sweep the court clean, and give the realm peace!" He Jin looked, and it was the son of Yuan Feng, Minister of the Masses, and nephew of [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei): [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) by name, Benchu by style, at that time Director of Retainers. He Jin was delighted, and mustered five thousand of the Imperial Guard. Yuan Shao put on full armor, and He Jin led in more than thirty great officers, He Yong, [Xun You](char-xun-you) and Zheng Tai among them, one after another. Before [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling)'s coffin they raised the heir apparent [Bian](char-prince-bian) to the throne.

When the officials had made their acclamation and their bows, [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) went into the palace to take [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo). Jian Shuo fled in a panic into the imperial garden, where the Attendant [Guo Sheng](char-guo-sheng) killed him in the shade of the flowers. The guards Jian Shuo had commanded all came over. "The eunuchs are a faction," said Yuan Shao to [He Jin](char-he-jin). "The chance is here today. Destroy them all." [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the others saw their danger and hurried in to [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he). "It was Jian Shuo alone who laid the plot against the Grand General at the beginning, and no business of ours. Now the Grand General listens to Yuan Shao and would destroy us all. We beg Your Majesty's pity!" "Have no fear. I will protect you." She sent out word summoning He Jin, and spoke to him privately. "You and I came of poor and humble stock. Without Zhang Rang and the rest, how could we have come to this wealth and honor? Jian Shuo was the wicked one, and he has paid for it. Why do you listen to others and want every eunuch killed?"

When she had finished, [He Jin](char-he-jin) went out and told the officers: "[Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) plotted against my life, and his family shall be destroyed to the last of them. There is no need to harm the rest." [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) said: "If the grass is cut and the root left, it will be the death of you." "My mind is made up. No more of it." And they all withdrew.

Next day the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) made [He Jin](char-he-jin) joint head of the Secretariat and gave office to all the rest. [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) called [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the others in to take counsel. "It was I who raised He Jin's sister up in the beginning. Today her child sits on the throne, and every officer within the palace and without is of the He family's party. Their power is too great. What am I to do?" Zhang Rang said: "Your Majesty may hold court and govern from behind the screen. Raise the prince [Xie](char-prince-xie) to a princedom, give the Imperial In-law [Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong) high office and the command of troops, and put us in places of trust. Then the great design can be carried through."

[Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) was delighted. Next day she held court and issued a decree making [Xie](char-prince-xie) Prince of Chenliu and [Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong) General of Agile Cavalry, and giving [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the rest a share in the government. [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he), seeing Empress Dowager Dong take all power into her own hands, set out a feast in the palace and invited her to it. When the wine was half done she rose, lifted her cup, bowed twice, and said: "We are both of us women. It is not fitting that we should meddle in government. In the old days [Empress Lü](char-empress-lu) held great power, and a thousand of her clan were put to the sword for it. We should keep to the deep seclusion of the palace and leave the great affairs of the court to the ministers and elders to settle, for the state's good. I beg you to hear me." Empress Dowager Dong said in a fury: "You poisoned Lady Wang out of a jealous heart. Now you lean on your son's throne and your brother [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s power, and dare to speak out of turn! I have only to order the General of Agile Cavalry to take your brother's head off, and it is done as easily as turning over a hand!" Empress Dowager He, angry in her turn, said: "I gave you good counsel. Why round on me for it?" "Butchers' and wine sellers' brats! What understanding should you people have?"

The two Empresses Dowager fell to quarreling, and [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the rest persuaded them each back to her own apartments. That night [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he) called [He Jin](char-he-jin) in and told him what had passed. He Jin went out and called the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers) into council. At the morning court the officers were to memorialize that [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong), being by origin the consort of a provincial marquis, ought not to live on in the palace, but should be moved to Hejian and settled there, and should be out of the capital that same day. Men were sent to start her on the road; at the same time palace guards surrounded the house of [Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong), General of Agile Cavalry, and demanded his seal of office. Dong Zhong saw how it stood and cut his own throat in the back hall. His household raised the wailing for him, and only then did the soldiers draw off. Zhang Rang and [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), seeing the Dong branch broken, set about winning over He Jin's younger brother [He Miao](char-he-miao) and his mother, the Lady of Wuyang, with gifts of gold, pearls and curiosities, so that they would go in to the Empress Dowager morning and evening and cover for them with fair words. So the Ten Attendants came back into favor.

In the sixth month [He Jin](char-he-jin) had [Empress Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) poisoned secretly at the posting house at Hejian, brought her coffin back to the capital, and buried her at Wenling. He then pleaded sickness and kept indoors. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), Director of Retainers, came in to see him. "[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) have put it about that you poisoned the Empress Dowager and are plotting to seize power. Destroy the eunuchs now, or great harm will come of it later. Dou Wu meant to destroy them once; his plan leaked, and the ruin fell on him instead. Today the officers and troops under you and your brother are all able men, and if you set them to it the work is as good as done. Heaven is giving you the moment, and it must not be let slip." "Let me think it over," said He Jin. One of those about him reported it privately to Zhang Rang, who passed it to [He Miao](char-he-miao) with more bribes, and He Miao went in to [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he). "The Grand General, who should be supporting the new sovereign, shows no mercy and thinks of killing only. Now he would kill the Ten Attendants too, with no cause at all. This is the road to disorder." And she listened to him.

Not long after, [He Jin](char-he-jin) came in to tell the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) that he meant to destroy the eunuchs. "It is the old usage of Han that the eunuchs have charge of the palace," she said. "The late Emperor has only just left the world, and you would put the old servants to death. That is no way to honor the ancestral temple." He Jin was by nature irresolute; he heard her out, said yes, and came away. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) met him and asked how the great business stood. "The Empress Dowager will not have it. What is to be done?" "Summon the bold men of the provinces and bring their troops to the capital, and destroy the eunuchs to the last. With matters so urgent, the Empress Dowager will not be able to refuse." "An excellent plan!" said He Jin, and sent out the call to the garrisons to come up to the capital.

[Chen Lin](char-chen-lin) the Registrar spoke against it. "It will not do! The proverb says that to cover your eyes and catch sparrows is to cheat yourself. If even so small a creature cannot be caught by deceit, how much less the great business of the state? General, you have the imperial authority behind you and the forces in your hand; you have a dragon's majesty and a tiger's stride, and may raise or cast down whom you will. To destroy the eunuchs would be no more than fanning a great furnace to singe a hair. You have only to strike quickly, use your power and decide at once, and Heaven and men will be with you. But to send out a call and bring the great men of the provinces up against the gates of the capital, where the bold will gather, each with a mind of his own, is what they call holding a sword by the blade and offering another the hilt. It cannot succeed, and will breed disorder instead." [He Jin](char-he-jin) laughed. "A coward's view!" Then a man at his side clapped his hands and laughed aloud. "It is as easy as turning over a hand. Why so much talk?" It was [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). Truly:
> Would he sweep out the knaves that vex the throne,
> He must heed counsel wiser than his own.
What Cao Cao had to say, the next chapter will tell.
